introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - Ordinary Level Examination. Computer Science (0595), Paper 3 (practical), June 2025. Duration: two and a half hours. Do all the tasks (Task I, Task II, Task III) specified in this question paper.**

The booklet reproduced here contains four versions of the same practical paper, headed Group One, Group Two, Group Three and Group Four (booklets 00/0595/3/Grp 1, Grp 2, Grp 3 and Grp 4). Each version has three tasks: Task I (word processing, 20 marks), Task II (spreadsheet, 20 marks) and Task III (reading and running a short C or Pascal program, 10 marks). A candidate works on one group only.

Enter the information required in the shaded boxes. For your guidance, the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All written answers should be provided in the spaces provided in this question booklet. Calculators are NOT allowed.

The working files named in the tasks (documents, workbooks and pictures supplied in the candidate folder) are supplied on the day; they are not reproduced in the printed paper.

questions.enonce_markdown: Launch either a C or Pascal program development environment, and key in the corresponding program. Do not key in the line numbers, which have been provided for convenience. Compile the program. If any errors, keep correcting and compiling until the errors are all corrected. Save as Task 3.  *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Open a C or a Pascal development environment installed on the computer (an editor with a compiler), create a new source file, key in the program of your choice **exactly as printed** without the line numbers, and compile it (*Build* / *Compile*, often F9). Save the file as **Task 3** (the extension `.c` or `.pas` is added by the environment).

- Check each detail while typing: `#include <stdio.h>`, the braces `{ }` and the semicolons in C; `begin ... end.` with the final full stop, `:=` for assignment and the semicolons in Pascal; the quotation marks and `&a`, `&b`, `&c` in `scanf`.
- Read the messages of the compiler: if it reports an error, go to the line indicated, correct it and compile again until no error remains.

*Marking idea (3 marks):* program keyed correctly (1); compiled without error (1); saved as Task 3 (1).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Run the program three times with inputs **40 20 10**, **20 40 10**, and **20 20 10** respectively. Write in the space below, the three output lines in which the results of the computations are displayed  *[3 marks]*

Input 40 20 10: ................

Input 20 40 10: ................

Input 20 20 10: ................
questions.corrige_markdown:
The program reads `a`, `b`, `c`, computes the average of the three numbers and their product, and displays **only one** of them, depending on the test `a > b`. Trace (same logic simulated in Python):

| Input a b c | a > b ? | Average (a+b+c)/3 | Product a x b x c | Line displayed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 40 20 10 | 40 > 20: true | 70/3 = 23.33 | 8000 | `Average: 23.33` |
| 20 40 10 | 20 > 40: false | 23.33 | 8000 | `Product: 8000` |
| 20 20 10 | 20 > 20: false | 50/3 = 16.67 | 4000 | `Product: 4000` |

- Input 40 20 10: **Average: 23.33**
- Input 20 40 10: **Product: 8000**
- Input 20 20 10: **Product: 4000**

Note the third run: a and b are equal, so `a > b` is false and the **else** branch (the product) is executed. (The three values are typed one per line, each after its prompt, so that `read` and `readln` of the Pascal program take one value each.)

*Marking idea (3 marks):* one mark per correct line.

questions.enonce_markdown: Explain what the program is designed to do.  *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The program asks the user for **three whole numbers** a, b and c. It calculates both their **average** (the sum divided by 3, stored in a real/float variable) and their **product**. It then **compares a and b**: if a is greater than b it displays the average (to 2 decimal places); otherwise (a smaller than or equal to b) it displays the product.

*Marking idea (2 marks):* reads three numbers and computes average and product (1); displays the average if a > b, otherwise the product (1).

questions.enonce_markdown: Explain the effects of **%.2f** (in line 14 of the C program) or **:0:2** (in Line 15 of the pascal Program)  *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Both are **formats for a real number**. In C, `%.2f` prints a floating-point number with **exactly 2 digits after the decimal point** (rounded): 23.333334 is displayed as **23.33**. In Pascal, `avg:0:2` gives the same result: the first number, **0**, is the minimum field width (no leading spaces are added) and the second number, **2**, is the number of **decimal places** (fixed-point notation instead of the scientific notation that Pascal uses for a real number written without a format).

Without them, C would display six decimal places (`%f` gives 23.333334) and Pascal would show the average in scientific notation, which is hard to read.

*Marking idea (2 marks):* two decimal places (1); explanation of the rounding / fixed-point display or of the 0 width in Pascal (1).
